units.t: Adulting 101. Episode one.
In this episode: Cooking fundamentals, Laundry done right, Home maintenance basics and Hiring a tradie without regrets.
Part one. Cooking fundamentals.
You don't need recipes to cook well.
You need to understand salt, fat, acid, heat and a few core techniques.
Principles over recipes.
Recipes are useful, but confident cooks understand principles.

Chef and author Samin Nosrat boiled good cooking down to four elements in her book Salt Fat Acid Heat: salt enhances flavour, fat carries flavour and creates texture, acid balances and brightens, and heat transforms food.
Once you understand them, you can improvise and rescue a bland dish.
The best habit is to taste as you go.
Salt makes food taste more like itself and reduces bitterness.
Season in stages, because salt added early has time to penetrate.
Salt pasta water generously.
Salting meat 40 minutes to a day ahead keeps it juicy and seasoned.
Still moderate your overall salt intake; much of it comes from processed foods.
Choosing your fat.
Different fats suit different jobs.
Butter tastes wonderful, but its milk solids start to burn at around 150 degrees.
For high-heat searing, add it near the end or use ghee, clarified butter with the milk solids removed, which copes with far more heat.
Neutral oils such as peanut or canola suit woks and deep-frying.
Smoke point isn't the whole story.
Laboratory studies, including Australian research, have found extra virgin olive oil among the most stable oils under heat, likely helped by its natural antioxidants.
Fat also builds texture: cold butter rubbed into flour makes flaky pastry.
And never pour used oil down the sink, where it sets and clogs pipes.
Low and slow.
Choosing the right heat starts with the cut.
Lean, tender cuts such as fillet, loin and chicken breast have little connective tissue.
They suit quick, hot methods like grilling and pan-frying, and dry out if cooked too long.
Hard-working muscles such as beef shin, chuck, brisket and lamb shoulder are full of collagen, a tough connective protein.
Cooked gently in liquid for hours, collagen slowly melts into gelatine, giving meat that falls apart and a silky sauce.
Keep a braise at a bare simmer, not a rolling boil, which tightens the muscle fibres and dries the meat.
If a stew is still tough, it usually needs more time, not more heat.
Prepare, then improvise.
Mise en place is French for 'everything in its place', and it separates calm cooks from frantic ones.
Before any heat goes on, read the whole recipe, then wash, chop, measure and line up every ingredient.
Chef Anthony Bourdain called it the religion of all good line cooks.
It matters most for fast cooking like stir-fries, and reading ahead catches surprises such as meat that needs marinating overnight.
Rather than collecting hundreds of recipes, master a few templates.
Stir-fry: hot pan, protein, vegetables, a sauce of soy, garlic, ginger and something sweet or sour.
Tray bake: vegetables and protein roasted with oil, salt and spices at about 200 degrees.
Soup: soften onion and garlic, add vegetables, stock and beans, simmer.
And eggs.
Swap freely and taste as you go.
Finishing well.
Food doesn't stop cooking when it leaves the heat.
The hot outer layers push heat inward, so a steak's centre climbs a few more degrees as it sits, and a big roast more.
This carryover cooking is why cooks pull meat slightly early.
Resting also keeps meat juicier.
Rest a steak about five minutes and a roast ten to twenty, loosely covered with foil.
A meat thermometer removes the guesswork.
For pasta, stir well in the first minute or two, when it is stickiest; oil in the water doesn't help.
Stop when it's al dente, tender with a slight bite.
Scoop out a cup of cooking water, then finish the pasta in the pan with the sauce and splashes of that starchy water so it turns glossy and clings.
The key idea: Good cooking rests on salt, fat, acid and heat, and salt works best added in stages while you taste.
Part two. Laundry done right.
Shrunken jumpers, pink socks and towels that smell faintly of damp are all avoidable.
A few habits will make your clothes last longer and your washing cheaper.
Labels, sorting and prep.
Flip a shirt inside out and you will find a small label of symbols.
Most people ignore it, which is how a favourite wool jumper ends up fitting a child.
The tub shows washing, with a number or dots for maximum temperature and a hand for hand washing.
The triangle is bleaching, the square drying, the iron ironing, and a circle alone means dry cleaning.
A cross through any symbol means do not.
Sort whites, lights and darks, since one new red t-shirt can turn a load of undies pink.
Wash new dark items alone for the first few washes, when excess dye is most likely to run.
Empty pockets, zip up zips, and put delicates in a mesh bag.
Turn dark clothes and prints inside out.
Cold water, right dose.
Most of the energy a washing machine uses on a warm or hot cycle goes into heating the water.
Modern detergents are designed to work well in cold water, so for everyday loads a cold wash is usually enough and costs much less.
Save warm or hot washes for greasy stains, towels and bedding, if the care label allows.
More detergent does not mean cleaner clothes.
Too much does not rinse out properly, leaving clothes stiff, dull and itchy, and residue can build up in the machine and cause smells.
Follow the dose on the pack.
Clothes also need room to move.
For a front loader, leave a hand's width at the top of the drum.
Tiny half loads waste water and electricity.
Drying without damage.
Australia's sunshine makes the clothesline one of the best appliances in the house, and it costs nothing to run.
Sunlight helps freshen whites, though strong sun can fade dark and bright colours, so hang those inside out or in the shade.
Hang clothes by their strongest seams to cut down on ironing.
Dry knitted wool flat on a towel, because hanging it wet can stretch it out of shape.
Clothes dryers are handy on wet days, but heat and tumbling are the main causes of shrinkage and wear, and dryers use a lot of electricity.
Heat pump dryers use considerably less than standard vented ones.
Clean the lint filter every single load.
Built-up lint makes the dryer work harder and is a recognised fire risk.
Keep the machine fresh.
If clean washing smells musty, the problem may be the machine.
Front loaders have rubber door seals that trap water, lint and detergent, creating a cosy home for mould and bacteria.
After each wash, leave the door and detergent drawer slightly open so the inside can dry.
Wipe the seal regularly, checking the folds for hair, coins and grime.
Every month or so, run an empty hot wash, using a washing machine cleaner if you like.
Many machines have a dedicated drum clean cycle.
Clean the filter too, if it is accessible, following the manual.
Take wet clothes out promptly.
Washing left sitting in the drum for hours is a fast route to that damp, sour smell.
Fixing common mistakes.
Even careful people end up with a pink load now and then.
If dye has run, do not put the clothes in the dryer.
Rewash them straight away in cold water, or use a supermarket colour run remover, following the instructions and checking the care labels first.
White items can often be soaked in an oxygen bleach solution.
Shrunken wool is harder.
Heat and agitation lock wool fibres together in a process called felting, which is permanent.
Soaking the garment in lukewarm water with a little hair conditioner and gently stretching it while damp can sometimes win back a little size, but there are no guarantees.
For stubborn smells in towels and sportswear, a hot wash with less detergent, plus thorough drying in the sun, often does more than adding fragrance.
The key idea: Read the care label, sort your washing, and prepare each load before it goes in.
Part three. Home maintenance basics.
Ten minutes a month and a few checks a year prevent the expensive, and dangerous, problems.
Renters, this is for you too.
Shut-offs and safety switches.
The time to find your water shut-off valve is not when a pipe has burst.
Locate three things now: the water main tap, usually near the water meter at the front of the property; the switchboard and main switch; and, if you have gas, the meter and its shut-off valve.
Show everyone in the household, and keep a working torch you can find in the dark.
A safety switch, or residual current device, RCD, cuts power in a fraction of a second if electricity leaks, for example through a person.
Test it every three months by pressing the 'T' button; power to those circuits should cut off, then flip the switch back up.
If it doesn't trip, call a licensed electrician.
Fire safety.
Working smoke alarms save lives, and they're required by law in Australian homes.
Test each one monthly by pressing the test button, and vacuum dust from the vents occasionally.
Replace alarms that are 10 years old or more; the date is usually printed on the alarm.
Fire services recommend photoelectric alarms, ideally interconnected so they all sound together, in bedrooms, hallways and on every level.
Rules differ by state; Queensland, for example, is phasing in interconnected photoelectric alarms in every bedroom.
Clear the clothes dryer's lint filter every load, because lint build-up is a common cause of house fires.
Water, mould and gutters.
A dripping tap can waste thousands of litres a year, and a hidden leak can cause major damage.
To check, turn off every tap, note the water meter reading, wait an hour without using water and check again.
If it has moved, you have a leak.
Watch for damp patches, bubbling paint, musty smells or high bills, and replace worn silicone around showers and baths.
Mould thrives on moisture and poor airflow.
Run the bathroom exhaust fan during and after showers, open windows, dry clothes outside and fix leaks promptly.
Large or recurring mould may mean a hidden leak that needs a professional.
Clean gutters before storm and bushfire seasons: blocked ones overflow into roofs and walls, and dry leaves are an ignition risk from embers.
Call a professional.
Plenty of jobs are fine to DIY: painting, changing tap washers, patching small holes, assembling furniture.
But electrical work, gas fitting and most plumbing must be done by licensed tradespeople in Australia, for good safety reasons.
Be especially careful when renovating homes built before 1990, which may contain asbestos in walls, eaves, floors and roofing.
Disturbing it can release deadly fibres.
If you're not sure, get it tested before drilling, cutting or sanding.
Check the roof for loose tiles or sheets after big storms from the ground, with binoculars, rather than climbing up.
And always check for underground services through Before You Dig Australia before digging.
Renters: know your rights.
If you rent, most repairs are the landlord's responsibility, but you need to report them.
Always report problems in writing, such as by email, and keep copies.

Every state distinguishes urgent repairs, like a burst water pipe, gas leak, dangerous electrical fault or broken hot water system, which must be fixed quickly, from general repairs, which must be done within a reasonable time.
Take dated photos at the start of your lease for your condition report.
Your state's tenancy authority has free guides and advice.
The key idea: Know where your water main, switchboard and gas shut-off are, and test your safety switches every three months.
Part four. Hiring a tradie without regrets.
Most tradies are honest, skilled and busy.
A few simple checks help you find them, and avoid the small number who leave a trail of half-finished jobs.
Licence and recommendations.
In every Australian state and territory, electrical work must be done by a licensed electrician, and gas fitting and most plumbing by licensed tradespeople.
Building work above a certain value also generally requires a licensed builder.
Each state's regulator runs a free online register where you can check a licence is current, what it covers and any disciplinary actions.
Ask for the number and check it yourself.
Also confirm public liability insurance.
The best leads come from neighbours, friends and family who had similar work recently.
Choose detailed reviews and be wary of a burst of short, glowing ones.
Ask about similar jobs, who will do the work and whether subcontractors are involved.
Someone vague, who never returns calls or will not put things in writing is unlikely to change.
Quotes, contracts and deposits.
For more than a small job, get at least three written quotes.
A quote sets out the work, materials, total price, whether GST is included and how long it is valid.
An estimate is only a best guess, and the bill can legitimately end up higher.
Make sure every quote covers the same scope.
The cheapest may leave out rubbish removal or quality materials.
Agree changes in writing, with the price, before they are done.
Above certain values, a written contract is generally required, setting out the work, price, timeframes and dispute handling.
Read it before signing.
Several states cap the deposit a builder can ask for on domestic work, commonly at around 10 per cent or less.
For bigger projects, tie payments to completed stages, not calendar dates, which matters if the business collapses partway.
Insurance that protects you.
Most states require builders to take out home warranty insurance, known by different names, on residential jobs above a set value.
It typically covers you if the builder dies, disappears or becomes insolvent and cannot finish the work or fix defects.
The builder must usually give you the certificate before taking a deposit or starting work, so ask to see it.
Separately, tell your own home and contents insurer about major renovations, as some policies change cover while building work is under way.
The tradie's public liability insurance covers damage they cause to your property or injuries to other people, so check that it is current too.
Red flags.
Be very wary of anyone who knocks uninvited, especially after a storm or flood, claiming your roof or gutters urgently need work.
Under consumer law, agreements made after an uninvited approach generally come with a cooling-off period of 10 business days.

Other red flags include pressure to sign today, a quote far below everyone else's, no ABN, no fixed address, refusal to give a written quote and a request for most of the money up front, especially in cash.
Cash with no invoice leaves you with no proof of what was agreed.
Pay by traceable methods, keep every receipt and never hand over the full amount before the job is finished.
When things go wrong.
Under the Australian Consumer Law, services must be provided with due care and skill, be fit for any purpose you made clear, and be delivered within a reasonable time if no deadline was agreed.
If something is not right, raise it calmly and promptly, ideally while the tradie is on site, then follow up in writing with photos.
Give them a fair chance to fix it, because most will.
If they will not, contact your state's fair trading office or building regulator, which can often help resolve disputes.
Some states run building dispute services, and civil tribunals can decide claims.
Keep a folder of quotes, contracts, messages, invoices and photos from the start.
Good records are your strongest tool.
The key idea: Check a tradie's licence on the official register and choose people through trusted recommendations.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why is it better to season in stages and salt meat well ahead of cooking?
Answer. Early salt has time to penetrate the food.
Question two. When are new dark clothes most likely to run dye?
Answer. In the first few washes.
Question three. How should you test a safety switch, RCD?
Answer. Press the test button every three months.
Question four. How should you check a tradie's licence?
Answer. Look it up on your state regulator's free register.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
